**Two-tower retrieval is fast because the item representation does not depend on the current user.** Compute every item's vector in advance, index those vectors, and compute one query/user vector per request. A dot product then gives a score compatible with efficient nearest-neighbor search. [1](https://research.google/pubs/sampling-bias-corrected-neural-modeling-for-large-corpus-item-recommendations/)

Now add “this user's historical CTR on this author.” The same author has a different value for each user, and the same user has a different value for each author. It is inherently a property of the pair. Putting it into the item tower would require recomputing that item's vector for each user, defeating the shared catalog index. Putting one candidate-specific value into the user tower would require a different query vector for each candidate.

**Use the cross-feature once the candidate set is small.** A pre-ranker or heavy ranker can fetch that user-author statistic for hundreds of retrieved items and evaluate rich interactions directly. Retrieval can still approximate the preference using separate user-interest and author/content embeddings.

The restriction is about arbitrary joint features, not every mathematical interaction. A structured feature that factorizes into independently computed terms may fit the two-tower score. Check that factorization explicitly. Also keep query and item encoder versions compatible: even correctly separated towers can fail if the index contains vectors from an incompatible model version.

**Technical details and references.**

A standard two-tower score factorizes as $f(user)^Tg(item)$ so item vectors can be computed once and indexed. A feature depending jointly on this user and this candidate cannot generally be evaluated inside either independently precomputed tower without breaking that separation. [1](https://research.google/pubs/sampling-bias-corrected-neural-modeling-for-large-corpus-item-recommendations/)

For example, “this user's historical CTR on this author” changes with both sides. Introduce it after candidate retrieval in pre-ranking/heavy ranking, or approximate it through separately encoded user-author preferences. Some structured interactions can be algebraically factorized or stored in user features, so the prohibition is not absolute for every cross-feature.

Verify index freshness and query/item encoder version compatibility. Adding arbitrary pairwise features to retrieval would require scoring the whole catalog or a different indexing strategy, defeating the intended scalability.
